A Type IV contingency measure sets branch weights to zero on all branches that do not experience thermal overloads for a set of contingencies. The Type IV contingency measure is useful for selecting single contingencies that when taken in combination could produce critical multiple contingencies.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The electricity consumption impacts of commercial energy management systems
abstract: An investigation of energy management systems (EMSs) in large commercial and institutional buildings in North Carolina was undertaken to determine how EMSs currently affect electricity consumption and what their potential is for reducing on-peak electricity demand. A survey was mailed to 5000 commercial customers. The 430 responses were tabulated and analyzed, EMS vendors were interviewed, and 30 sites were investigated in detail. The detailed assessments included a site interview and reconstruction of historic billing data to evaluate EMS impact, if any. The results indicate that a well-tuned EMS can result in a 10 to 40% reduction in billed demand, and smaller reductions in energy consumption.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Interactive data management system for power system planning studies
abstract: An interactive data management system is presented which provides efficient facilities for centralized administration and handling of the bulk of data required for power system planning studies. The system is interfaced to a group of analytical programs and integrated into the GINA (graphics-aided interactive network analysis) power system analysis package. The data management system operates in a user-friendly environment provided by the use of graphical routines, menus of option, and an online system. Efficient organization of the filing system provides economical storage of the information combined with satisfactory retrieval speed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: WEMAP-a computer aided instructional tool for electromagnetics
abstract: WEMAP is an electromagnetic analysis computer code for teaching electromagnetics to power engineering students. WEMAP is a stand-alone interactive graphics system for electromagnetic analysis, which includes electrostatics, magnetostatics, eddy currents (time harmonic as well as transient), and permanent magnet fields. These capabilities are described, and examples are given to illustrate how this program can enhance the classroom presentation of some of the electromagnetic phenomena.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Current electric system operating problems from a cogenerator's viewpoint
abstract: Power system operating problems are presented from a cogenerator's viewpoint, considering steam power constraints of the cogeneration process, control of tie-lines to cogeneration plants, voltage support, emergency response, and maintenance. Also discussed are the technical planning problems associated with system protection, underfrequency load shedding, and the need for long-term operations planning. As the amount of cogeneration increases in the electric utility industry, additional concerns arise regarding various purchase and sale contracts and administration requirements for both the cogenerator and the electric utility.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improvements in sparse matrix/vector technique applications for online load flow calculation
abstract: Several analytical and computational improvements in sparsity applications are discussed. A novel partial matrix refactorization method and ordering algorithm are presented. The method is very efficient when applied to programs such as online load flow, optimal power flow, and steady-state security analysis. It is applied in a fast decoupled load flow program which includes the treatment of tap violations on underload tap changing transformers and reactive power generation on PV buses. The effects of proposed improvements are tested and documented on a 118-bus IEEE test network and two utility networks with 209 and 519 buses, respectively.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Backup control centers: justification, requirements, emergency planning, and drills
abstract: This report is one of a series of presented on behalf of the IEE Power Engineering Society's System Operations Subcommittee with the intent of focusing industry attention on current problems faced by electric utilities in the operation of the bulk power supply system. Six short note reports are presented which direct attention to problem areas in disaster planning and, in particular, establishing backup control centers. The first report addresses the sensitive issue of assessing the risks associated with not having a backup center and of justifying its costs. The second report identifies the functional capabilities required of a backup control center and illustrates the wide range of implementation choices. The third report describes the communications strategies and facilities that are necessary. The fourth report develops a set of criteria to be utilized for facility requirements and site selection. The fifth report addresses emergency planning requirements. The final report explains the challenges in developing, testing, and updating control center evacuation procedures.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modeling of generating unit planned outages in the decomposition-simulation approach for multi-area reliability calculations
abstract: A brief description of the extended decomposition-simulation approach is presented. An algorithm is then described for generating unit planned outage modeling in the extended decomposition-simulation approach for multiarea reliability calculations. The algorithm is based on a single-step decomposition of the state space and greatly reduces the computational requirements of the approach while producing accurate results. System studies are presented to illustrate the use of the algorithm.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A method to eliminate solution trapping in applying progressive optimality principle to short-term hydrothermal scheduling
abstract: A method is described to eliminate solution trapping for the POP (progressive-optimality-principle) based short-term hydrothermal scheduling algorithm. In a POP-based scheduling algorithm, the trapping phenomenon can severely hinder solution optimality and thus limits the algorithm's applicability. In order to ensure path continuity, the proposed method identifies and bypasses the potential weak links, so that global optimality can be achieved progressively by successively solving a sequence of two-hour subproblems. Examples are given to illustrate the trapping phenomenon and the proposed method.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Probabilistic generating capacity cost of service allocation
abstract: A procedure is presented for cost-of-service allocation at hierarchical level I (HLI) which utilizes a probabilistic technique similar to that used by many utilities for generating-capacity planning. The procedure is illustrated by application to the IEEE Reliability Test System (RTS). A brief introduction to the deterministic techniques presently utilized by most utilities in HLI cost-of-service allocation is provided. The results obtained by applying selected methods to the IEEE RTS are illustrated and compared.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Adoption of electromagnetic transients program (EMTP) on personal computers
abstract: The electromagnetic transients program (EMTP) was downloaded from mainframe to a computer. The details of compiling, linking, memory requirements, and execution time for a mainframe and a personal computer running this software are compared. Two case studies are presented comparing the performances of EMTP on a mainframe and a personal computer. This research establishes the viability of using this software on a personal computer for power system transient computations. Appreciable memory savings are found in the PC version. The compiling time for the software in the PC is found to be around two hours. The run times for programs are found to be satisfactory. Directions for future research are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Risk and benefits assessment of long and short term capacity contract strategies
abstract: A planning methodology is developed for purchasing firm capacity. The methodology evaluates the risk and benefits associated with long- and short-term capacity contracts. It facilitates the selection of a contract strategy that satisfies the capacity requirements of a utility company within its financial and operating constraints. In simplified form the issue addressed in this study is when a utility company should sign its next capacity contract, for how many megawatts, at what price, and for what duration.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Operating economy benefits of improved gas turbine reliability
abstract: The potential operating economy benefits of improved reliability for generating plants using advanced gas turbines in integrated gasification combined cycle and simple cycle applications are evaluated using an expanded probabilistic production cost model. Results obtained for four reduced EPRI regional model systems indicate that initial capital investments in the range of $2 to $7 million dollars per gas turbine could be economically justified by future operating cost savings. The study also explores the expected cost per failure event and per MWh of energy not supplied by the gas turbine due to forced plant outages. These results are shown to be highly dependent on the fuel and capacity mix of the system as well as on the forecasts of fuel price differences.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Current operating problems associated with non-utility generation
abstract: This paper is one of a series presented on behalf of the Systems Operations Subcommittee with the intent of focusing industry attention on current problems faced by electric utilities in the operation of its bulk power systems. Four short note reports are presented with direct attention to problem areas being faced by utilities in regard to nonutility generation systems. Each report focuses on different aspects of the nonutility generation problem. The reports address generation and fuel, transmission, distribution, and energy management and control systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An evaluation of alternative load measurement frameworks for resource planning
abstract: Three alternative frameworks for counting loads and resources to be used for resource planning purposes are reviewed, and their implications are evaluated using an example taken from a recent planning exercise. They are: the traditional approach, which focuses on utility sales to ultimate customers; the California Energy Commission (CEC) approach, which includes more self-generation and conservation and load management (C&LM) programs; and the inclusive approach, which adds savings from all existing programs in both historic and future periods. The three approaches are applied to an actual case. The author recommends a compromise between the current CEC framework and the inclusive framework as the best balance of benefits and costs for resource planning purposes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Spreadsheet approach to production costing-case study for a municipal utility
abstract: A case study is presented of a municipal utility using electronic spreadsheets for production costing. The data are used as a testbed for comparing alternative techniques for handling forced outages, including Monte Carlo methods, probability generating functions, and an enumerative approach. The spreadsheet models are validated by comparison with an established mainframe program, EPRI's BENCHMARK. The results demonstrate clearly the importance of modeling economy sales on the spot market in assessing the overall costing performance of utilities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Operational losses savings attributable to load management
abstract: The reduction of customer load by means of a utility-controlled switch is discussed that results in a reduction of losses throughout the distribution and transmission systems, including the transformers between the load and the generation sources. Two methods of calculating the losses savings are described that both require that losses be expressed as a function of load. The recommended function is a quadratic equation. One method begins with hourly production loads (the total generation plus purchases minus sales), determines the customer level loads by the application of the quadratic equation to calculate the losses, subtracts the controlled load, and recalculates losses. This procedure is easily computerized and can be used in conjunction with standard industry production costing and generation expansion models. The second method, based on marginal or incremental calculation techniques using the quadratic equation, is moire amenable to one-time applications such as in a specific hour.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The use of load and billing data to design cost-based agricultural rates
abstract: The process through which PG&E rate analysis identified problems in the old rate structure and set about rectifying them is discussed. Both load research data and billing data, together with market intelligence from the agricultural sector, were central to quantifying problem areas and posing and testing new rate structures. It is shown how load and billing data can be effectively used to develop new schedule revenue allocations and schedule rate designs that are closely based on marginal costs and flexible enough to provide a range of time-differentiated rates designed to satisfy different segments of the agricultural electricity marketplace.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A listing of continuing education courses in electric power engineering-1988
abstract: This second subcommittee report is based on an updated survey of continuing education courses/seminars in electric power engineering currently offered by universities and industry in the USA. It is meant to provide a convenient database for power engineers and other professionals wishing to enhance their skills through continuing education. For each organization that responded to the survey, the report contains a listing of course titles, duration, and continuing education credit, if awarded, as well as a concise statement of the purpose of each course and for whom the course is intended.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
